extracted.intended_audience: general readers and those interested in history/World War II/Holocaust studies
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic article analyzing the forgery of Hitler's diaries by Konrad Kujau, showing how the fake texts were constructed, how they trivialize the Holocaust, and how experts detected the falsification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification and trivialization of history
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts immediately recognized both the falsification and trivialization of history, as well as the Holocaust denial embedded into the fake diaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess texts for deliberate misrepresentation or minimization of historical crimes (e.g., wording that downplays murder, reframes genocidal policy as benign). The page cites Hajo Funke and Heike Görtemaker identifying these features in Kujau's diaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political motivation / neo-Nazi affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The forger's political motives and affiliations are part of the evaluation: Kujau repeatedly described himself as a neo-Nazi and associated with right-wing extremists who helped write the diaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the forger's biography and contacts (e.g., reports of Hitler salutes, SS garb, SS ring, collaboration with ANS/NA member Lothar Zaulich) to determine ideological intent behind the forgery rather than purely financial motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of minor changes to disguise original source
rubrics_metrics.description: By making minor changes, Kujau hoped to disguise the original source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for near-verbatim borrowings from primary documents with only small lexical or contextual alterations (e.g., slight rewordings of lines from the Wannsee protocol) indicating copying rather than independent composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution of protocol language to Hitler
rubrics_metrics.description: Kujau places phrases nearly identical to the Wannsee protocol into Hitler's diary entries, changing speaker/context so protocol material appears as Hitler's own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare suspect diary passages directly to known primary-source documents (e.g., Eichmann/Wannsee protocol); flag passages that lift summarized protocol language and present it as Hitler's personal statements or thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context shifting to alter meaning (trivialization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases from the Wannsee protocol are relocated into different contexts in the diaries to change their implication (e.g., making Hitler appear unaware of or opposed to murder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether quoted or paraphrased material has been moved from an administrative/meeting context into a personal-diary context in ways that invert or soften original intent. The page gives examples where genocidal intent is reframed as logistical or benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical and factual adjustments to conceal borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Kujau slightly alters figures and facts (e.g., reducing 'over 11 million' to 'over 10 million') to obscure direct copying from the protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check numerical data and factual details against source documents; small, systematic adjustments can indicate an attempt to mask plagiarism or direct lifting of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronistic or historically implausible portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: The fake diaries present historically implausible scenes (e.g., Hitler 'eagerly awaiting' Wannsee outcomes) that contradict what is known about the roles of participants and the nature of the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plausibility against the established historical record (who would realistically await what, which actors were responsible for decisions). Implausible characterizations can signal fabrication or poor historical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling errors and linguistic inconsistencies as forgery markers
rubrics_metrics.description: The diaries contain numerous spelling mistakes and awkward phrasing (noted with [sic]), which are highlighted in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographical errors, unusual phrasing, and inconsistent language as supporting evidence of inauthenticity—especially when such errors appear in passages otherwise closely echoing formal primary-source prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and handling irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems in chains of custody and publisher handling (e.g., disappearance into Stern's archives, failure to deliver to Federal Archives, eventual online publication by NDR) are part of the evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how documents were acquired, stored, and transferred; unexplained disappearances, delayed transfers to official archives, or nonstandard publication routes warrant skepticism about authenticity.
